p.src: Baoyu looked up and saw that Shui Rong, Prince of Beijing, wore a spotless white princely cap with jeweled tassels and silver wings, a white python robe embroidered with river cliffs, ocean waves, and a seated five-clawed dragon, and a red leather belt adorned with jade. His face was as fair as beautiful jade and his eyes shone like bright stars; he was truly a handsome and elegant figure. Baoyu hastened forward to pay his respects, but Shui Rong quickly reached out from his sedan chair and took him by the hand. He saw that Baoyu wore a silver crown over his bound hair, a forehead band embroidered with twin dragons rising from the sea, a white python-patterned archer's jacket, and a silver belt studded with clustered pearls; his face was like a spring blossom and his eyes like dots of glossy lacquer. Shui Rong smiled. “Your reputation does not belie you: you are indeed as precious as treasure and as fair as jade.” Then he asked, “Where is the precious object you were born holding in your mouth?” At this question, Baoyu quickly took it from inside his clothes and handed it to him. Shui Rong examined it closely and read the inscription upon it, then asked, “Does it truly possess miraculous powers?” Jia Zheng hurriedly replied, “So it is said, but it has never been put to the test.” While exclaiming over its marvelous strangeness, Shui Rong straightened its colored cord and personally fastened it on Baoyu. Then, still holding his hand, he asked his age and what books he was studying. Baoyu answered each question in turn.

p.src: Finding his speech clear and his conversation graceful, Shui Rong smiled at Jia Zheng and said, “Your son is truly a young dragon colt and phoenix chick. I do not mean to speak presumptuously before you, venerable sir, but in time ‘the young phoenix's voice may ring clearer than the old phoenix's’; his future is beyond measure.” Jia Zheng hastened to smile deferentially. “How could my unworthy son presume to receive Your Highness's lavish praise? If, through the lingering blessings of Your Highness's princely house, he should indeed fulfill your words, it would be the good fortune of all of us who live under its protection.” Shui Rong continued, “There is only one concern. With gifts such as your son's, the venerable old lady and the ladies of the family naturally must dote on him exceedingly. Yet young men like us ought not to be overindulged, for excessive affection inevitably leads us to neglect our studies. I myself once followed that very path, and I imagine your son may not be entirely free of the same tendency. If he finds it difficult to apply himself at home, let him visit my humble residence often. Though I possess little talent, I have been favored by many distinguished scholars from across the land, and whenever they come to the capital, none fails to show me particular regard. Consequently, quite a number of eminent men gather at my residence. If your son comes often to converse and associate with them, his learning may improve day by day.” Jia Zheng bowed and readily assented.

p.src: Shui Rong then removed a string of prayer beads from his wrist and handed it to Baoyu. “This is our first meeting, and in the haste of the occasion I have brought no suitable congratulatory gift. These fragrant wagtail-wood prayer beads were personally bestowed upon me by His Majesty the other day; please accept them for the present as my gift.” Baoyu quickly accepted the beads, then turned and presented them to Jia Zheng. Jia Zheng and Baoyu thanked the prince together. Jia She, Jia Zhen, and the others then came forward together to ask the prince to return to his sedan. Shui Rong said, “The departed has already ascended to the realm of immortals and is no longer one of the ordinary mortals who inhabit this dusty world. Though I have undeservedly received Heaven's favor and inherited a princely title in name, how could I presume to pass ahead of an immortal's hearse?” Seeing that he firmly refused, Jia She and the others had no choice but to take their leave, thank him for his graciousness, and return. They ordered the musicians to cover their instruments and cease playing, and the vast funeral procession streamed past in its entirety before Shui Rong was allowed to return to his sedan and depart. There is no need to dwell upon this further.

p.src: Now, the Ning household's funeral procession continued on its way amid extraordinary bustle and splendor. Just as they reached the city gate, memorial pavilions erected by the households of Jia She, Jia Zheng, and Jia Zhen's various colleagues and subordinates received the procession with offerings. After thanking each in turn, the party left the city and proceeded directly along the highway toward Iron Threshold Temple. At that point Jia Zhen brought Jia Rong before their elders and invited them to mount their sedan chairs or horses. Thus Jia She's generation entered their carriages and sedan chairs, while Jia Zhen's generation prepared to mount their horses. Xifeng, however, was worried about Baoyu. She feared that once in the countryside he might give free rein to his willfulness, act recklessly, and refuse to listen to the servants. Jia Zheng did not attend to such trifles, and she dreaded that some mishap might occur, leaving her unable to face Grandmother Jia; she therefore sent a page to summon him. Baoyu had no choice but to come to her carriage. Xifeng laughed. “Dear brother, you are a person of noble birth and as delicately made as a girl. Do not imitate those fellows and perch on horseback like a monkey. Come down. Would it not be better for the two of us to ride together in the carriage?” On hearing this, Baoyu quickly dismounted and climbed into Xifeng's carriage, and the two traveled on laughing and chatting. Before long, two riders came thundering toward them from the other direction. Near Xifeng's carriage, both leapt from their horses, took hold of the carriage, and reported, “There is a resting place here. Madam may stop to rest and change her clothes.” Xifeng immediately ordered them to ask Lady Xing and Lady Wang for instructions. The messenger returned and said, “Their Ladyships say they have no need to rest and that Madam may do as she pleases.” On hearing this, Xifeng ordered that they stop to rest before continuing. The pages obeyed, turned the shaft horse aside from the crowd, and sped northward. From inside the carriage, Baoyu urgently ordered them to invite young Master Qin. Qin Zhong was then riding beside his father's sedan chair when he suddenly saw Baoyu's page run up and invite him to join them for refreshment. Looking over, Qin Zhong saw Xifeng's carriage heading north with Baoyu's horse being led behind it, the saddle cover draped over the saddle. He realized that Baoyu was riding with Xifeng, so he too led his horse after them and entered a farmstead with the others. The household servants had already driven all the farmhands away. The peasant household had few rooms, however, so the women had nowhere to withdraw and could only be left where they were. When the village girls and farm women beheld Xifeng, Baoyu, and Qin Zhong—their looks and clothing, their polished manners and elegant bearing—how could they help wanting to gaze at them?

p.src: Presently Xifeng entered the thatched hall and told Baoyu and the others to go outside and amuse themselves first. Baoyu understood her meaning and went out with Qin Zhong, taking the pages with them to explore and play here and there. They had never seen any of the implements used by farming households. When Baoyu saw such things as spades, stakes, hoes, and ploughs, he found them all remarkable, knowing neither what each was used for nor what it was called. The pages beside him named them one by one and explained their uses. Hearing this, Baoyu nodded and sighed, “No wonder the old poem says, ‘Who knows that every grain upon the plate was won by bitter toil?’ This is exactly what it means.” Still talking, they came to another room, where Baoyu saw a spinning wheel on the kang and asked the pages, “And what is this?” The pages again explained it to him. On hearing them, Baoyu stepped forward and turned the wheel for sport, finding it highly amusing. Just then a village girl of about seventeen or eighteen came running over and cried in alarm, “Don’t touch it—you’ll break it!” The pages hurriedly shouted at her and barred her way. Baoyu quickly let go and said with an apologetic smile, “I had never seen one before, so I only wanted to try it.” The girl said, “You people don’t know how to work it. Stand aside, and I’ll spin for you to see.” Qin Zhong secretly tugged at Baoyu and laughed, “This young lady is most intriguing.” Baoyu thrust him away and laughed, “You wretch! Talk such nonsense again and I’ll hit you.” As he spoke, the girl began to spin thread. Just as Baoyu was about to speak, an old woman called from the other side, “Second Girl, come here quickly!” Hearing the call, the girl abandoned the spinning wheel and went straight off.

p.src: Baoyu was left disappointed and dispirited. Then Xifeng sent someone to summon the two of them inside. Xifeng washed her hands, changed her clothes, and shook off the dust, then asked whether they wished to change too. Baoyu declined, so she let the matter drop. The household women brought out the travelling teapot and cups, tiered boxes filled with assorted delicacies, and various refreshments. After Xifeng and the others had taken tea and the servants had packed everything away, they rose and boarded the carriages. Outside, Wang’er had prepared a gratuity in a red packet, which he presented to the master of the village household. The village women came to kowtow in thanks for their rewards. Xifeng paid them no heed, but when Baoyu looked carefully, Second Girl was not among them. Once they had boarded and travelled a short distance, they saw Second Girl coming toward them with her little brother in her arms, laughing and talking with several younger girls. Baoyu longed to jump down and follow her, but knew that the others would never permit it, so he could only watch her recede. Yet the carriage was light and the horses swift, and in the blink of an eye she had vanished from sight.

p.src: Before long, they caught up with the great funeral procession once more. Ahead, Dharma drums and brass cymbals were already sounding amid banners, pennants, and ceremonial canopies: all the monks of Iron Threshold Temple had come to receive the spirit. Soon they entered the temple, where fresh Buddhist rites were performed and the incense altar was set up anew. The spirit was installed in a side chamber of the inner hall, while Baozhu was lodged in an inner sleeping room to keep it company. Outside, Jia Zhen entertained all the relatives and friends. Some stayed to eat, while others took their leave without dining. After the customary courtesies, the guests departed group by group, from dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons downward; it was near the end of the wei hour before the last had gone. Inside, Xifeng managed the reception of all the female guests. The titled wives of the highest officials were the first to leave, and it was well past noon before the last of them had departed. Only a few of the closest relatives remained, intending to leave after the three-day service for the repose of the spirit. Madam Xing and Madam Wang knew that Xifeng would certainly be unable to return home, so they prepared to go back into the city. Madam Wang wished to take Baoyu with her, but having only just reached the countryside, he refused to go back and insisted on staying with Xifeng. Madam Wang could do nothing but entrust him to Xifeng and return home. Iron Threshold Temple had originally been built by the Dukes of Ning and Rong. It still possessed incense lands donated for its upkeep, so that elderly members of the clans in the capital might conveniently have their coffins lodged there. Both the quarters for the dead and those for the living had been properly prepared, providing lodging for those accompanying a funeral. But as later generations multiplied, differences of wealth and clashes of temperament arose among them. Those of modest means who were content with their lot stayed here; those with money and influence who still cared for display declared the place inconvenient and insisted on finding lodgings elsewhere, either in a country house or a convent, where they could rest and hold their concluding feast when the ceremonies were over. For the present funeral of Madam Qin, all the clansmen were temporarily lodged at Iron Threshold Temple. Xifeng alone found it inconvenient, and had therefore sent someone ahead to speak with Abbess Jingxu of Steamed-Bun Convent and have two rooms vacated for her lodging. Steamed-Bun Convent was in fact Water-Moon Convent. Because its steamed buns were so good, it had acquired this nickname. It stood not far from Iron Threshold Temple. By then the monks had finished their offices and the offerings of tea and rice had been made, so Jia Zhen ordered Jia Rong to invite Xifeng to retire and rest. Seeing that several of her sisters-in-law remained to attend the female relatives, Xifeng took leave of the company and set out for Water-Moon Convent with Baoyu and Qin Zhong. Qin Ye, being old and often ill, had been unable to attend; he had merely instructed Qin Zhong to remain until the spirit was settled. Qin Zhong therefore simply accompanied Xifeng and Baoyu. When they reached Water-Moon Convent, Jingxu came out to welcome them with her two disciples, Zhishan and Zhineng, and they all exchanged greetings. After Xifeng and the others had entered a clean room, changed their clothes, and washed their hands, Xifeng noticed that young Zhineng had grown still taller and prettier. She therefore said, “Why have neither you nor your mistress visited us lately?”

p.src: Jingxu said, “I have had no time these past few days. A son was born in Master Hu’s household, so Her Ladyship sent ten taels of silver here and asked several of the sisters to recite the Blood-Basin Sutra for three days. I have been so busy that I have not had a moment free and could not come to pay my respects to you.” We shall leave the old nun attending Xifeng for the moment. Meanwhile, Qin Zhong and Baoyu were amusing themselves in the main hall. When Baoyu saw Zhineng approaching, he laughed and said, “Here comes Neng’er.” Qin Zhong said, “Why pay any attention to that creature?” Baoyu laughed. “Do not play tricks with me. That day in the Old Lady’s room, when no one else was there, what were you embracing her for? And now you are still trying to deceive me.” Qin Zhong laughed. “Nothing of the sort ever happened.” Baoyu laughed. “Whether it happened or not is no concern of mine. Just call her back and have her pour me a bowl of tea, and I will let the matter drop.” Qin Zhong laughed. “That is a strange request. Ask her to pour it yourself—surely she will not refuse you. Why must I say it?” Baoyu said, “If I ask her, the tea will be poured without affection; if you ask her, it will be poured with affection.” Qin Zhong had no choice but to say, “Neng’er, bring me a bowl of tea.” Zhineng had frequented the Rong Mansion since childhood and was known to everyone there, for she often joked and played with Baoyu and Qin Zhong. Now that she was older and had begun to understand affairs of the heart, she had taken a fancy to the elegant and charming Qin Zhong; Qin Zhong, for his part, was greatly enamored of her beauty and allure. Though nothing had yet passed between them, their hearts were already one. Now, at the sight of Qin Zhong, Zhineng’s whole heart brightened, and she went to pour the tea. Qin Zhong said with a smile, “Give it to me.” “Give it to me!” cried Baoyu. Zhineng pursed her lips in a smile. “Quarreling over a single bowl of tea! Do you imagine I have honey on my hands?” Baoyu snatched it first and began drinking. He was just about to ask her something when Zhishan came and called Zhineng away to set out the tea dishes; shortly afterward, someone came to invite the two boys to take tea, fruit, and refreshments. The two of them had no appetite for such things; after sitting for a little while, they went out to play again.

p.src: After sitting a little while longer, Xifeng returned to the quiet room to rest, escorted by the old nun. By then, the matrons and married servants, seeing that there was nothing more to do, had dispersed one after another to rest. Only a few trusted young maids remained in attendance. Seizing her opportunity, the old nun said, “There is a matter for which I intend to petition Her Ladyship at your mansion, and I should first like to ask for your guidance.” Xifeng asked what the matter was. The old nun said, “Amitabha! When I first took religious vows at Shancai Convent in Chang’an County, there was a wealthy patron there by the surname of Zhang. He had a daughter whose childhood name was Jinge. One year, when the family came to burn incense at my convent, she happened to meet Young Master Li, the brother-in-law of the Prefect of Chang’an. Young Master Li fell for Jinge at once and was determined to marry her, so he sent a matchmaker with a proposal. But Jinge had already been formally betrothed to the son of the former garrison commander of Chang’an. The Zhang family feared that the commander would not consent if they broke the engagement, and so they replied that she was already promised to another. But Young Master Li stubbornly refused to accept this and insisted on marrying their daughter. The Zhang family could think of no solution and found themselves caught between the two sides. When the commander’s family heard of this, they disregarded right and wrong, came to abuse and insult the Zhangs, accused them of promising one daughter to several families, and flatly refused to take back the betrothal gifts. They even began legal proceedings against them. Driven to desperation, the Zhang family had no choice but to send someone to the capital to seek influential help, determined out of sheer defiance to return the betrothal gifts and break the engagement. It occurred to me that Governor Yun, the military commissioner of Chang’an, is on the most intimate terms with your household. Her Ladyship might ask His Lordship to write him a letter, requesting him to have a word with the former commander. Then the commander would hardly dare refuse. If this can be arranged, the Zhang family would gladly spend their entire fortune to show their gratitude.”

p.src: Xifeng listened and said with a smile, “The matter is not especially difficult, but Her Ladyship never involves herself in affairs of this kind.” The old nun said, “Even if Her Ladyship will not intervene, you could take the matter in hand yourself.” Xifeng laughed upon hearing this. “I am not in want of silver, nor do I engage in such dealings.” Jingxu abandoned her hopes and, after a long pause, sighed. “That may be so, but the Zhang family already knows that I have come to petition your household. If the matter is now refused, they will not understand that you are too busy to attend to it or that you have no interest in their gift of thanks. They will only think that your great household lacks the means to accomplish even such a trifling thing.”

p.src: These words roused Xifeng’s pride. She said, “You have known me long enough. I have never believed in retribution from the courts of the underworld or the torments of hell. Whatever the affair may be, if I say it shall be done, it shall be done. Tell them to bring three thousand taels of silver, and I shall avenge this affront for them.” The old nun was beside herself with joy and hurriedly said, “Yes, yes! That will present no difficulty.” Xifeng continued, “I am not like those brokers and go-betweens who do such things for the sake of money. Those three thousand taels are merely to cover the traveling expenses of the page sent with the message and to let him earn a little for his trouble. I shall not take a single coin of it. Why, I could produce thirty thousand taels myself this very moment.” The old nun readily assented and added, “In that case, it would be a great kindness if you would grant them your favor tomorrow.” Xifeng said, “Just look how busy I am—which place can manage without me? But since I have promised you, naturally I shall settle it as quickly as possible.” The old nun said, “Such a little affair would keep anyone else so busy that they would not know where to turn; but before you, even several more matters like it would hardly suffice to display your abilities. Still, as the proverb says, ‘The capable must labor the more.’ Her Ladyship sees how perfectly you manage affairs great and small and so entrusts them all to you without reserve. You must take care of your precious health.” Flattered all the way by these words, Xifeng grew ever more pleased; forgetting her weariness, she continued chatting with the nun.

p.src: As it happened, Qin Zhong took advantage of the darkness and the absence of others to seek out Zhineng. No sooner had he reached the rear room than he saw Zhineng there alone, washing teacups; Qin Zhong rushed over, threw his arms around her, and kissed her. Zhineng stamped her foot in distress and said, “What do you think you’re doing! If you do that again, I’ll scream.” Qin Zhong pleaded, “My dear, I’m dying of longing. If you still refuse me today, I’ll die right here.” Zhineng said, “What do you want? Only after I escape this prison and leave these people behind will I consent to you.” Qin Zhong said, “That can easily be arranged, but distant water cannot quench an immediate thirst.” With that, he blew out the lamp, plunging the room into utter darkness, carried Zhineng onto the kang, and began making love to her. Zhineng struggled in every way but could not break free, and as she dared not cry out, she had no choice but to yield to him. Just as they were in the midst of their pleasure, someone entered, pinned them both down, and said not a word. Not knowing who it was, they were so terrified that neither dared move a muscle. Then the intruder gave a snort and could no longer suppress his laughter; hearing the voice, they realized it was Baoyu. Qin Zhong hurriedly got up and complained, “What do you think you’re doing?” Baoyu laughed. “If you won’t agree, then let’s start shouting.” Mortified, Zhineng slipped away under cover of darkness. Baoyu pulled Qin Zhong outside and said, “Will you still try to defy me?” Qin Zhong laughed. “My dear fellow, just don’t let everyone know. Whatever you want, I’ll agree to it.” Baoyu laughed. “There’s no need to say anything now. Once we’re in bed, I’ll settle accounts with you properly.” When it was time to undress and retire, Xifeng slept in the inner room, while Qin Zhong and Baoyu slept in the outer room; the floor everywhere was occupied by old serving women who had spread out bedding and were sitting up on night watch. Fearing that the Precious Jade of Spiritual Understanding might be lost, Xifeng waited until Baoyu was asleep, then ordered someone to bring it to her and tucked it beside her own pillow. What account Baoyu settled with Qin Zhong is not clearly known or remembered; it remains a doubtful matter, and I dare not fabricate an account of it.

p.src: The night passed without further incident. Early the next morning, Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang sent servants to see Baoyu, instructing him to put on a couple more layers and, if there was nothing requiring his presence, to come home. Baoyu, however, had no intention of returning; and Qin Zhong, reluctant to leave Zhineng, urged Baoyu to ask Xifeng to stay another day. Xifeng considered the matter: although all the important funeral arrangements were settled, a few minor details remained unattended to, and she could use these as a reason to stay another day. Would that not, first, display the full measure of her devotion before Jia Zhen; second, allow her to complete the business entrusted by Jingxu; and third, gratify Baoyu, which would surely please Grandmother Jia when she heard of it? Seeing these three advantages, she said to Baoyu, “My own business is finished, but if you want to amuse yourself here, I suppose I shall have to put myself to the trouble of staying one more day. Tomorrow, though, we must certainly leave.” Hearing this, Baoyu called her “dearest sister” over and over as he pleaded, “Only one more day—we’ll be sure to go home tomorrow.” And so they stayed another night.

p.src: Xifeng then had the matter concerning the old nun the previous day quietly explained to Laiwang. Laiwang understood everything at once. He hurried into the city, found a secretary skilled in drafting documents, and, claiming that Jia Lian had instructed him, had a letter composed. He traveled through the night to Chang’an County, no more than a hundred li away, and within two days the entire affair was settled. The military governor, whose name was Yun Guang, had long been indebted to the Jia household; how could he possibly refuse so small a request? He supplied a letter in reply, and Laiwang returned with it. But no more need be said of that for now.

p.src: To resume: Xifeng and the others stayed one more day and did not take leave of the old nun until the following day, telling her to come to the mansion three days later for news. Qin Zhong and Zhineng could scarcely bear to part. How many secret trysts and private vows they arranged behind others’ backs need not be related in detail; at last, they could only part in sorrow. Xifeng also went to Iron Threshold Temple to look things over once more. Baozhu adamantly refused to return home, so Jia Zhen had no choice but to assign some women to keep her company. We shall meet them again in the next chapter.
